questions.q: What loop does this lesson explicitly close from earlier in this same course?
options: Chapter 3, Lesson 11's four-component portfolio structure, told to a learner about to build the capstone that didn't exist yet at the time
A loop opened in Chapter 2's job-market lessons about consulting versus in-house roles
A loop that has nothing to do with any earlier lesson in this course
Chapter 1's comparison of CSA, CAD, CIS, and CTA credentials
questions.explain: Lesson 11 taught the four-component structure and told the learner they were about to apply it to a capstone starting in Chapter 4 -- this lesson is that promised application.

questions.q: Which statement correctly fills in this capstone's "business problem" component, per this lesson's own standard?
options: "Built a Flow Designer flow and a REST integration"
"Used ServiceNow for a help desk project"
Three consolidating hospital systems had no shared way to log or route IT tickets, each with real trust in its own process, against a board deadline and reporting requirements that couldn't be broken
"Implemented best practices for ITSM"
questions.explain: Lesson 11 required the business problem stated as a real situation, not a feature list -- the other options are exactly the feature-list framing it warned against.

questions.q: Which of this chapter's own decisions is an example filling Lesson 11's "design decisions and why" component?
options: The choice to use ServiceNow instead of a competing platform
The choice to defer HR service delivery and facilities management to a later phase
The hospital systems' original help-desk categorization habits before this project started
The scheduled, fifteen-minute Prairie View worker sync, chosen over forcing a new webhook build or a manual CSV process, with its staleness-window tradeoff named honestly
questions.explain: This is a real alternative-weighing decision with a stated tradeoff -- exactly the ADR discipline Lesson 11 asked candidates to apply to their own capstone.

questions.q: What is the honest answer to Lesson 11's "what would you do differently at scale" component for this specific capstone?
options: Nothing would need to change; the build is already production-ready at 5,000 users
The capstone has no real scale limitations worth naming

Name specific gaps honestly -- the Prairie View sync needs load-testing at real volume, the Workday and ADP integrations still need to actually be built, and the new escalation group needs real staffing
Scale limitations only apply to the integration lessons, not the rest of the build
questions.explain: Lesson 11 said naming real limits honestly is a stronger answer than pretending a lab-scale build was already production-ready -- this lesson applies that directly to the Meridian capstone.

questions.q: Why does Lesson 11 say "what was actually built" matters least of the four portfolio components, and this lesson treats it the same way?
options: Because the build doesn't need to be mentioned in a portfolio write-up at all
Because an interviewer can often see the build for themselves if it's being demoed, so the write-up's real job is the reasoning around it, not narrating every click
Because what was built is actually the most important of the four components
Because nothing was actually built in this capstone
questions.explain: Lesson 11 was explicit that the build itself should stay factual and short in the write-up, since it's often visible directly -- the reasoning components carry the real weight.
